massospondylus:enwiki:3.title: Massospondylus (Owen's 1854 description and loss of the type material)

massospondylus:enwiki:5.title: Massospondylus (Previously recognised species from southern Africa)

facts.statement: The genus Massospondylus includes the type species M. carinatus and the species M. kaalae.
facts.quote: taxon: Massospondylus

facts.statement: Massospondylus was described by Richard Owen in 1854 based on fossils found in South Africa.
facts.quote: It was described by Richard Owen in 1854 from remains discovered in South Africa

facts.statement: Massospondylus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages of the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: The genus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages

facts.statement: Most Massospondylus fossils are found in the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho.
facts.quote: Most fossils come from the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho

facts.statement: Massospondylus fossils have also been found in the Forest Sandstone and Mpandi Formation of Zimbabwe.
facts.quote: the genus is also found in the Forest Sandstone and the Mpandi Formation of Zimbabwe

facts.statement: Massospondylus is now considered to have been bipedal, despite earlier depictions of it as quadrupedal.
facts.quote: Although Massospondylus was long depicted as quadrupedal (four-legged), it is now considered to have been bipedal (two-legged)

facts.statement: Massospondylus was probably a herbivore, though some researchers speculate that basal sauropodomorphs may have been omnivorous.
facts.quote: This dinosaur was probably a herbivore (plant-eater), although some have speculated that basal sauropodomorphs may have been omnivorous

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a sharp thumb claw on each hand, likely used for feeding by uprooting vegetation or pulling down branches.
facts.quote: On each of its hands, it bore a sharp thumb claw that was probably used in feeding, possibly to uproot vegetation or to pull down branches while rearing up

facts.statement: Fossils of Massospondylus include clutches of eggs containing embryos, representing some of the oldest amniote eggs and embryos known.
facts.quote: Clutches of eggs have been found, some of which contained embryos; these are among the oldest eggs and embryos of an amniote in the fossil record

facts.statement: The eggshells of Massospondylus were extremely thin, measuring less than 0.1 mm, unlike the thicker shells of later dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The eggshell was extremely thin, less than 0.1 mm, unlike the much thicker eggshells in later dinosaurs

facts.statement: The oldest known Massospondylus specimen reached an age of around 20 years.
facts.quote: The oldest known specimen was around 20 years of age

facts.statement: The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by Richard Owen in 1854.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by Richard Owen in 1854

facts.statement: The Hunterian Museum in London, which held the original Massospondylus collection, was destroyed by a bomb on the night between May 10 and 11, 1941.
facts.quote: The museum was damaged during several nearby bombings before it was directly hit by a bomb on the night between May 10 and 11, 1941

facts.statement: It is debated whether Owen's assignment of bones to Massospondylus, Pachyspondylus, or Leptospondylus was arbitrary, a view supported by Hans-Dieter Sues in 2004.
facts.quote: Hans-Dieter Sues found to be somewhat arbitrary in 2004

facts.statement: Researchers Paul Barrett and Kimberley Chapelle speculated that early neglect of Massospondylus species was due to Richard Owen's perfunctory descriptions lacking illustrations.
facts.quote: Paul Barrett and Kimberley Chapelle speculated was due to Owen's "rather perfunctory descriptions", which lacked illustrations

facts.statement: A British-South African expedition discovered a Massospondylus hatchling skeleton at Mafeteng, Lesotho, in 1961, though it was initially misidentified as Heleosaurus.
facts.quote: Already in 1961, a British-South African palaeontological expedition discovered the skeleton of a hatchling (SAM-PK-K413) at Mafeteng, Lesotho, although this specimen was first misidentified as the varanopid Heleosaurus.

facts.statement: Michael Cooper published a monograph in 1981 describing the Zimbabwean Massospondylus skeleton, noting that skull material was unavailable.
facts.quote: In 1981, Michael Cooper published a comprehensive monograph on the Zimbabwean Massospondylus material, describing the entire skeleton apart from the skull, of which no material was available.

facts.statement: Chris Gow and colleagues provided the first detailed description of the Massospondylus skull in 1990 using four specimens from the Evolutionary Studies Institute in Johannesburg.
facts.quote: The skull of Massospondylus was first described in detail in 1990 by Chris Gow and colleagues based on four well-preserved skulls housed at the Evolutionary Studies Institute in Johannesburg.

facts.statement: Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues published a comprehensive description of the four Massospondylus skulls and proposed the first formal diagnosis for M. carinatus in 2004.
facts.quote: In 2004, Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues provided a more comprehensive description of the same four skulls, and proposed the first diagnosis of M. carinatus (the set of distinguishing features).

facts.statement: Yates and Barrett proposed in 2010 to designate specimen BP/1/4934 as the neotype for Massospondylus because the original syntype series lacked distinguishing features.
facts.quote: Consequently, Yates and Barrett proposed in 2010 to designate a different specimen, BP/1/4934, as the neotype specimen (the new representative specimen).

facts.statement: The neotype specimen of Massospondylus, nicknamed "Big Momma," was found on a farm near Clocolan, South Africa, in March 1980 by Lucas Huma and James Kitching.
facts.quote: The specimen, nicknamed "Big Momma" although its sex is unknown, was found in March 1980 on a farm near Clocolan, South Africa, by Lucas Huma and James Kitching.

facts.statement: Chapelle and Jonah Choiniere described the skull of the "Big Momma" neotype in 2018, while Barrett and colleagues described the rest of the skeleton in 2019.
facts.quote: The skull was described in detail in 2018 by Chapelle and Jonah Choiniere, while Barrett and colleagues described the remainder of the skeleton in 2019.

facts.statement: As of 2019, the "Big Momma" specimen was the largest and most complete Massospondylus known, and likely the most complete basal sauropodomorph found in Africa.
facts.quote: As of 2019, it is the largest and most complete Massospondylus specimen and probably the most complete basal (early diverging) sauropodomorph specimen discovered in Africa.

facts.statement: The "Big Momma" specimen underwent extensive restoration in the 2000s because repeated handling caused deterioration of the fossils.
facts.quote: In the 2000s, the specimen was extensively restored after it became apparent that the fossils were deteriorating due to repeated handling.

facts.statement: Currently, two species of Massospondylus are recognized: the type species M. carinatus and M. kaalae.
facts.quote: Besides the type species Massospondylus carinatus, one additional species, Massospondylus kaalae, is currently recognised.

facts.statement: Barrett identified the skull as a new species in 2004 and formally named it M. kaalae in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2004, Barrett noted that this skull belonged to a new species, which he named M. kaalae in 2009.

facts.statement: The species M. kaalae was named in honor of Sheena Kaal, the museum's collections manager for Karoo vertebrate fossils.
facts.quote: The species is named in honor of the museum's collections manager for the Karoo vertebrate fossils, Sheena Kaal, for her assistance to numerous scientists who have studied specimens at the museum.

facts.statement: Harry Seeley tentatively named the species M. browni in 1895.
facts.quote: In 1895, Seeley named the species M. browni, although its assignment to Massospondylus was only tentative.

facts.statement: M. browni was based on vertebrae and limb bones discovered north of the Witteberg by Alfred Brown.
facts.quote: This species was based on two neck, two back, and three tail vertebrae as well as femora and toe bones that were discovered north of the Witteberg by Alfred Brown.

facts.statement: In 1906, Friedrich von Huene concluded that the material assigned to M. browni represented two separate species.
facts.quote: In 1906, von Huene concluded that the vertebrae and femora of M. browni belonged to two separate species.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton assigned to M. browni by van Hoepen in 1920 was later moved to M. harriesi and is now considered part of M. carinatus.
facts.quote: In 1920, Egbert Cornelis Nicolaas van Hoepen assigned a partial skeleton to M. browni, which was later assigned to M. harriesi and is now listed as a specimen of M. carinatus.

facts.statement: A 2004 review classified M. browni as an indeterminate sauropodomorph.
facts.quote: M. browni was considered an indeterminate sauropodomorph in a 2004 review by Peter Galton and Paul Upchurch.

facts.statement: Robert Broom named M. harriesi in 1911 based on forelimb and hind limb fragments found near Fouriesburg.
facts.quote: M. harriesi was named by Robert Broom in 1911 based on parts of a forelimb and hind limb discovered near Fouriesburg.

facts.statement: In a 2004 review, both M. harriesi and M. schwarzi were considered indeterminate sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: Both species were considered as indeterminate sauropodomorphs in the 2004 review.

facts.statement: Several South African species originally assigned to other genera were once considered synonyms of Massospondylus but are now regarded as indeterminate due to incompleteness.
facts.quote: Several other species from South Africa have originally been assigned to different genera, were later regarded as synonyms of Massospondylus, and are currently regarded as indeterminate (too incomplete to be classified).

facts.statement: Seeley named Hortalotarsus skirtopodus in 1894 based on a specimen from the Clarens Formation near Barkly East.
facts.quote: Hortalotarsus skirtopodus was named by Seeley in 1894, based on a specimen found in the Clarens Formation near Barkly East.

facts.statement: Broom named Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, and Gyposaurus capensis in 1911.
facts.quote: Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus and Gyposaurus capensis were all named by Broom in 1911.

facts.statement: Broom named Gryponyx transvaalensis in 1912 based on foot bones found in the Bushveld Sandstone Formation in Limpopo Province.
facts.quote: One year later, in 1912, Broom named Gryponyx transvaalensis from two foot bones (an ungual and a metatarsal) discovered in the Bushveld Sandstone Formation in Limpopo Province.

facts.statement: Haughton named Thecodontosaurus minor in 1918 based on a vertebra, tibia, and ilium from the Elliot Formation near Maclear.
facts.quote: Thecodontosaurus minor was named by Haughton in 1918 based on a neck vertebra, a tibia, and an ilium found in the Elliot Formation near Maclear.

facts.statement: Haughton named Thecodontosaurus dubius and Gryponyx taylori in 1924.
facts.quote: In 1924, Haughton erected another species of Thecodontosaurus, T. dubius, as well as Gryponyx taylori.

facts.statement: Galton and Cluver assigned several species to M. harriesi in 1976.
facts.quote: In 1976, Galton and Cluver assigned Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, Gryponyx taylori, Dromicosaurus gracilis, and Thecodontosaurus dubius to M. harriesi.

facts.statement: Michael Cooper considered all related taxa as synonyms of M. carinatus in 1981.
facts.quote: Cooper, in 1981, instead considered all taxa as synonyms of M. carinatus.

facts.statement: Opinions on synonymy changed over time, with a 1990 review listing some species as synonyms of M. carinatus, but a 2004 review classifying all as indeterminate sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: Galton, in a 1990 review, only listed Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, Gyposaurus capensis, and Gryponyx taylori as synonyms of M. carinatus, while the 2004 review considers all species to be indeterminate sauropodomorphs rather than synonyms of Massospondylus.

facts.statement: Researchers question whether all previously identified Massospondylus specimens from southern Africa belong to this genus due to the discovery of new genera.
facts.quote: During the 21st century, two additional massospondylid genera were identified in southern Africa, raising the question of whether all of the previous identifications of Massospondylus specimens were correct.

facts.statement: The genus Ignavusaurus was described in 2010 based on a juvenile specimen.
facts.quote: The first of these genera, Ignavusaurus, was described in 2010 from a juvenile specimen.

facts.statement: While Yates and colleagues considered Ignavusaurus a synonym of Massospondylus in 2011, later analyses by Chapelle in 2018 and 2019 classified it as a distinct massospondylid genus.
facts.quote: In 2011, Yates and colleagues considered it to be a probable synonym of Massospondylus, but cladistic analyses led by Chapelle in 2018 and 2019 recovered it as a distinct taxon of massospondylid.

facts.statement: The genus Ngwevu was described in 2019 based on fossils discovered in 1978 that were previously assigned to Massospondylus carinatus.
facts.quote: The second genus, Ngwevu, was described in 2019 by Chapelle and colleagues based on a complete skull with a fragmentary skeleton that had been discovered in 1978 and was previously assigned to M. carinatus.

facts.statement: In 2023, researchers concluded that a humerus from the upper Elliot Formation previously assigned to Massospondylus belongs to a new, unnamed, small sauropodomorph genus.
facts.quote: In 2023, Chapelle and colleagues concluded that a humerus from the upper Elliot Formation, which also had been provisionally assigned to Massospondylus, belonged to a new sauropodomorph genus that was unusually small.

facts.statement: Massospondylus fossils have been found in the Lower Maleri and Takli formations of India, the Kayenta Formation of the US, and the Cañón del Colorado Formation of Argentina.
facts.quote: Massospondylus has been previously recognised from outside of Africa, namely from the Lower Maleri and Takli formations of India, the Kayenta Formation of the US, and the Cañón del Colorado Formation of Argentina.

facts.statement: R. Lydekker described the species M. hislopi and M. rawesi in 1890 based on fossils found in India.
facts.quote: In 1890, Lydekker described the species M. hislopi and M. rawesi from fossils found in India.

facts.statement: M. hislopi was based on a fragmentary vertebra from the Lower Maleri Formation, while M. rawesi was based on a tooth found in the Upper Cretaceous Takli Formation.
facts.quote: M. hislopi was based on a single fragmentary vertebra from the Lower Maleri Formation in Andhra Pradesh, while M. rawesi was based on a single tooth found by Mr. Rawes in the Upper Cretaceous Takli Formation in Maharashtra.

facts.statement: In 1906, von Huene believed that M. hislopi and M. rawesi were not dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In 1906, von Huene believed that both species were not dinosaurs.

facts.statement: A 2004 review classified M. hislopi as an indeterminate sauropodomorph and M. rawesi as an indeterminate theropod.
facts.quote: M. hislopi was listed as an indeterminate sauropodomorph in a 2004 review by Galton and Upchurch but M. rawesi is an indeterminate theropod.

facts.statement: Fossils from India mentioned in 1987 as Massospondylus were reassigned to the family Guaibasauridae in 2011.
facts.quote: Other Massospondylus fossils from India were mentioned in 1987 by T.S. Kutty and colleagues but have instead been assigned to the family Guaibasauridae in 2011.

facts.statement: US material described in 1985 was assigned to the genus Sarahsaurus in 2010–2011.
facts.quote: The material from the US, which consists of a nearly complete skull with skeleton described in 1985, was assigned to the new and closely related genus Sarahsaurus in 2010–2011.

facts.statement: Argentinian material described in 1999 was recognized as the new genus Adeopapposaurus in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, the Argentinian material, which consists of several partial skeletons described in 1999, has likewise been recognised as a new genus, Adeopapposaurus.

facts.statement: Cooper suggested in 1981 that Yunnanosaurus and Lufengosaurus were synonyms of Massospondylus, but this view was not adopted by later researchers.
facts.quote: Cooper, in his 1981 study, suggested that the Chinese genera Yunnanosaurus and Lufengosaurus were synonyms of Massospondylus, which would have expanded its range to China. He classified Lufengosaurus as a separate species of Massospondylus, M. huenei. This suggestion was not followed by subsequent authors.

facts.statement: Massospondylus was a mid-sized sauropodomorph.
facts.quote: Massospondylus was a mid-sized sauropodomorph.

facts.statement: Barrett and colleagues estimated the large neotype specimen of Massospondylus to be around 5 meters long in 2019.
facts.quote: In 2019, Barrett and colleagues estimated the particularly large neotype specimen at around 5 m in length.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Massospondylus to be 4.3 meters long in a 2024 book.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul, in a popular book published in 2024, estimated Massospondylus to be 4.3 m in length.

facts.statement: Frank Seebacher estimated the body weight of Massospondylus at 136.7 kg in 2001, assuming a length of 4 meters.
facts.quote: The body weight was estimated at 136.7 kg by Frank Seebacher in 2001, assuming a body length of 4 m.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the body weight of Massospondylus at 195 kg.
facts.quote: Paul instead gave a body weight of 195 kg.

facts.statement: Unlike some basal sauropodomorphs like Plateosaurus, the vertebrae of Massospondylus lack signs of pneumaticity.
facts.quote: Although some basal sauropodomorphs such as Plateosaurus show incipient pneumaticity in their vertebrae, those of Massospondylus are apneumatic (lack any signs of pneumaticity).

facts.statement: The external nostril at the front of the skull was roughly half the size of the eye socket.
facts.quote: At the front of the skull was the large external naris (nostril), which was roughly half the size of the orbit (eye socket).

facts.statement: A small fenestra called the mandibular fenestra perforated the mandible.
facts.quote: A small fenestra, the mandibular fenestra, also perforated the mandible.

facts.statement: A distinguishing feature of the Massospondylus skull is that the basipterygoid processes form an angle of approximately 35 degrees, which is smaller than in other basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: A single distinguishing feature is found in the skull: the basipterygoid processes, a pair of bony extensions that braces the braincase against the palate, form an angle of ca. 35°, whereas this angle is much larger in all other basal sauropodomorphs in which it can be measured.

facts.statement: The premaxilla of Massospondylus consistently had four teeth on each side in all known skulls.
facts.quote: The premaxilla, the front bone of the upper jaw, showed the constant number of four teeth per side in all known skulls.

facts.statement: The number of teeth in the maxilla of Massospondylus varied between 14 and 22.
facts.quote: In the maxilla, the tooth count varied from 14 to 22.

facts.statement: Massospondylus teeth were replaced throughout life, creating a saw-like profile due to varying tooth heights.
facts.quote: The teeth were replaced throughout life, as in other dinosaurs. This resulted in neighbouring teeth being of different heights, giving the tooth row a profile similar to a saw.

facts.statement: A 2013 study estimated that Massospondylus teeth remained in use for only 17 to 30 days.
facts.quote: a 2013 study estimated that a tooth remained in use for only 17 to 30 days.

facts.statement: Front teeth of Massospondylus had pointed, slightly curved tips, while posterior teeth were spatulate and more symmetrical.
facts.quote: Teeth closer to the front of the snout had pointed tips and were slightly curved, unlike the posterior teeth that were spatulate (with a broad, flat tip) and more symmetrical.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a vertebral column consisting of nine neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae, three hip vertebrae, and at least forty tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column was composed of nine cervical (neck) vertebrae, 13 dorsal (back) vertebrae, three sacral (hip) vertebrae, and at least 40 tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: The front neck vertebrae of Massospondylus had elongated neural spines with a hook-like protuberance at the front end, distinguishing it from other basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: In the anterior cervicals, the neural spine (the bony keel that formed the top of each vertebra) was elongated, and its anterior end had a hook-like protuberance that constitutes another distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a shoulder blade with a symmetrical upper expansion, unlike related genera where the front expansion was much larger than the rear.
facts.quote: The shoulder blade had an expanded upper end. This expansion was more symmetrical than in related genera, in which the dorsal (front) expansion was much larger than the ventral (rear) expansion, and is a distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: The pubis bone in the hip of Massospondylus faced forward, similar to most saurischian dinosaurs.
facts.quote: In the hip, the pubis faced forward, as with most saurischians.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had forelimbs that were half the length of its hind limbs but were quite powerful due to a large deltopectoral crest on the humerus.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were only half the length of the hind limbs but quite powerful, as indicated by a broad flange on the upper portion of the humerus called the deltopectoral crest, which provided attachment areas for a large arm musculature.

facts.statement: The deltopectoral crest on the humerus of Massospondylus extended for approximately 60% of the bone's length, which is longer than in related genera.
facts.quote: This crest was longer than in related genera, extending for ca. 60% of the length of the bone, which is a distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: The ulna in Massospondylus measured around 60% of the length of the humerus, making the lower arm proportionally short.
facts.quote: The lower arm was proportionally short, with the ulna measuring around 60% of the length of the humerus, which is another distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of the hand in Massospondylus was 2-3-4-3-2.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula of the hand, which states the number of finger bones from the thumb to the fifth digit, was 2-3-4-3-2.

facts.statement: The foot of Massospondylus had a large, curved claw on the first digit that was flattened from side to side.
facts.quote: The foot also had a large claw on the first digit, which was curved and flattened laterally (side-to-side).

facts.statement: The claws on the middle three digits of Massospondylus were smaller, less curved, and flattened from top to bottom.
facts.quote: The claws on the middle three digits instead were smaller, less curved, and flattened dorsoventrally (top to bottom).

facts.statement: The fifth toe of Massospondylus consisted of a single bone and lacked a claw.
facts.quote: The fifth toe only had a single toe bone and no claw.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of the foot in Massospondylus was 2-3-4-5-1.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula of the foot was 2-3-4-5-1.

facts.statement: Massospondylus was described by Sir Richard Owen in 1854 from fossils discovered in South Africa, making it one of the first named dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Descrita por Sir Richard Owen en 1854 a partir de restos descubiertos en Sudáfrica, siendo uno de los primeros dinosaurios en ser nombrado.

facts.statement: Massospondylus lived during the early Jurassic period, between 200 and 183 million years ago, from the Hettangian to the Pliensbachian stages in Africa.
facts.quote: Massospondylus (del griego: "vértebra elongada") es un género extinto representado por dos especies conocidas de dinosaurios prosaurópodos masospondílidos que vivieron a principios del período Jurásico, entre 200 a 183millones de años, desde el Hettangiense al Pliensbachiense en África.

facts.statement: Fossils of Massospondylus have been found in various locations in South Africa, Lesotho, and Zimbabwe.
facts.quote: Fósiles de este han sido encontrados en distintos lugares de Sudáfrica, Lesoto y Zimbabue.

facts.statement: In 1920, von Huene named the group Prosauropoda to unite early long-necked dinosaurs including Massospondylus.
facts.quote: In 1920, von Huene named the new group Prosauropoda to unite the early long-necked dinosaurs including Massospondylus.

facts.statement: In 1932, von Huene named the group Sauropodomorpha, which included his Prosauropoda and Sauropoda, abandoning the traditional classification of Massospondylus within Theropoda.
facts.quote: In 1932, he also named the new group Sauropodomorpha, which contained his Prosauropoda as well as Sauropoda, abandoning the traditional classification of Massospondylus and related genera within Theropoda.

facts.statement: Massospondylidae has been recognized by a majority of studies as the family containing Massospondylus.
facts.quote: Massospondylidae has since been recognised by a majority of studies.

facts.statement: The genus Massospondylus was named by Owen in 1854.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Owen, 1854

facts.statement: The type species of Massospondylus is Massospondylus carinatus.
facts.quote: type_species: Massospondylus carinatus

facts.statement: Massospondylus belongs to the family Massospondylidae.
facts.quote: familia: Massospondylidae

facts.statement: Massospondylus kaalae is a subdivision of Massospondylus described by Barrett in 2009.
facts.quote: subdivision: Massospondylus kaalae Barrett, 2009

facts.statement: Synonyms for Massospondylus include Aetonyx (Broom, 1911), Aristosaurus (Hoepen, 1920), Dromicosaurus (Hoepen, 1920), Hortalotarsus (Seeley, 1894), Leptospondylus (Owen, 1895), and Pachyspondylus (Owen, 1854).
facts.quote: synonyms: Aetonyx Broom, 1911 Aristosaurus Hoepen, 1920 Dromicosaurus Hoepen, 1920 Hortalotarsus Seeley, 1894 Leptospondylus Owen, 1895 Pachyspondylus Owen, 1854

facts.statement: Several studies have classified Massospondylus within the Plateosauridae or the Anchisauridae family, creating debate over its exact family placement.
facts.quote: although several studies classified Massospondylus within the Plateosauridae or within another family, the Anchisauridae.

facts.statement: Massospondylus was a typical prosauropod with a moderately long neck and slender legs.
facts.quote: Massospondylus fue un típico prosaurópodo de cuello medianamente alargado y patas delgadas.

facts.statement: While once thought to be omnivorous, new discoveries indicate that Massospondylus was herbivorous.
facts.quote: Por un tiempo se creyó que Massospondylus era omnívoro pero ha habido nuevos descubrimientos que demuestran que era herbívoro.

facts.statement: Massospondylus swallowed stones to aid digestion, a behavior evidenced by gastrolites found in its stomach.
facts.quote: Para mejorar su digestión tragaba piedras, probado por la presencia de gastrolitos en su estómago, tal como lo hacían muchos sauropodomorfos.

facts.statement: Massospondylus possessed an acute claw on each front foot's thumb, used for defense or gathering food.
facts.quote: En cada una de sus patas delanteras poseía una garra aguda en el pulgar que fue utilizada en defensa o para recoger el alimento.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest Massospondylus exhibited continuous growth throughout its life, possessed bird-like air sacs, and may have cared for its young.
facts.quote: Estudios recientes indican que Massospondylus crecía constantemente a través de su vida útil, que poseía sacos de aire similares a los de las aves, y que pudo haber cuidado de sus crías.

facts.statement: Massospondylus reached approximately 4 meters in length and weighed about 135 kg, though some estimates suggest a length of 6 meters.
facts.quote: Este dinosaurio alcanzaba alrededor de los 4m, y peso aproximadamente 135kg, aunque algunas estimaciones sugieren unos 6m de largo.

facts.statement: While traditionally assumed to be quadrupedal, a 2007 anatomical study questioned this, arguing its limb range of motion prevented an efficient habitual quadrupedal gait.
facts.quote: Aunque siempre se ha asumido que habría sido cuadrúpedo, un estudio anatómico de sus miembros delanteros 2007 ha cuestionado esto, sosteniendo que su rango de movimientos imposibilitaba un habitual paso cuadrúpedo eficaz.

facts.statement: Despite its mass suggesting quadrupedalism, Massospondylus was likely a facultative biped.
facts.quote: Aunque su masa sugiera una naturaleza cuadrúpeda, realmente se trataría de un bípedo facultativo.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a slender body with a long neck consisting of about nine cervical vertebrae, thirteen dorsal vertebrae, three sacral vertebrae, and at least forty caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Poseía un cuerpo delgado con un cuello largo, con alrededor de nueve vértebras cervicales, trece dorsales, tres sacras y al menos 40caudales.

facts.statement: The pubis of Massospondylus extended forward, a trait shared by most saurischians.
facts.quote: El pubis se prolongaba hacia adelante, como en la mayoría de los saurisquios.

facts.statement: Recent discoveries show Massospondylus had a well-developed clavicle connected to a furcula, suggesting these bones held the scapula immobile and were not rudimentary or non-functional in dinosaurs lacking true wishbones.
facts.quote: Un reciente descubrimiento muestra que Massospondylus poseía un bien desarrollada clavícula, unida a una fúrcula, sugiriendo que ambos que sostenían inmóviles a la escápula y que las clavículas no eran rudimentarias y no funcionales en esos dinosaurios que no tenían espoletas verdaderas.

facts.statement: The small head of Massospondylus measured approximately half the length of the femur.
facts.quote: La pequeña cabeza de Massospondylus medía aproximadamente la mitad del largo del fémur.

facts.statement: Numerous openings, or fenestrae, in the skull of Massospondylus reduced weight and provided space for muscle insertion and sensory organs.
facts.quote: Numerosas aberturas, o fenestras, en el cráneo reducían el peso, suministrando espacio para la inserción de los músculos y los órganos de los sentidos.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had two large, elliptical nostrils at the front of its skull.
facts.quote: En el frente del cráneo había dos grandes y elípticas narinas.

facts.statement: The eye orbits of Massospondylus were proportionally larger compared to other genera like Plateosaurus.
facts.quote: Las órbitas oculares eran proporcionalmente grandes en Massospondylus comparadas con otros géneros como Plateosaurus.

facts.statement: Like other prosauropods, it has been proposed that Massospondylus possessed cheeks.
facts.quote: Como en otros prosaurópodos, se ha propuesto que Massospondylus tuviese mejillas.

facts.statement: Crompton and Attridge (1986) suggested Massospondylus had a beak to compensate for jaw malocclusion, but this was later shown to be an interpretation based on a skull with a dorsally crushed lower part.
facts.quote: Crompton y Attridge en 1986 describieron el cráneo de Massospondylus como poseedor de una maloclusión y sugiriendo la presencia de un pico córneo de queratina en la extremidad de la mandíbula inferior para suplir la diferencia en longitud y para explicar desgaste los dientes en la extremidad del hocico. Sin embargo, posteriormente se ha demostrado que fue una interpretación basada un cráneo con la parte inferior aplastada dorsalmente.

facts.statement: Massospondylus teeth near the front of the snout had rounded sections and sharp tips, while rear teeth were spatulate with oval sections.
facts.quote: Los dientes más cercanos al frente del hocico tenían secciones redondeadas y eran afilados en los extremos, mientras que los dientes traseros eran espatulados y tenían secciones ovales.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by paleontologist Sir Richard Owen in 1854, who named it from the Greek words for 'long' and 'vertebra'.
facts.quote: Los primeros fósiles de Massospondylus fueron descritos por el paleontólogo Sir Richard Owen en 1854, que le dio el nombre derivado de los términos del griego μάσσων, masson, "largo" y σπόνδυλος, spondylos, "vértebra".

facts.statement: Fossils of Massospondylus were found in 1853 by J. M. Orpen in the Upper Elliot Formation at Harrismith, South Africa.
facts.quote: Estos fósiles fueron encontrados en 1853 por J. M. Orpen en la Formación Elliot Superior en Harrismith, África del Sur.

facts.statement: Possible remains of Massospondylus have been found in the Upper Elliot Formation, Clarens Formation, and Bushveld Sandstone of South Africa and Lesotho, the Forest Sandstone and Upper Karroo Sandstone of Zimbabwe, and the Kayenta Formation of Arizona.
facts.quote: Posibles restos de Massospondylus han sido encontrados en la Formación Elliot Superior, Formación Clarens y Arenisca Bushveld de Sudáfrica y Lesoto, la Arenisca Forest y Arenisca Karroo Superior de Zimbabue y la Formación Kayenta de Arizona.

facts.statement: Recent re-studies of African Massospondylus skull specimens indicate that the Kayenta specimen does not belong to Massospondylus.
facts.quote: Recientes reestudios de los especímenes africanos de cráneos de Massospondylus, sin embargo, indican que el espécimen de Kayenta no pertenece a Massospondylus.

facts.statement: Massospondylus belongs to the parent group Massospondylidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Massospondylidae

facts.statement: Massospondylus is classified in the family Massospondylidae.
facts.quote: Family: Massospondylidae

facts.statement: Massospondylus is classified in the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: Massospondylus lived from the Carnian to the Toarcian stages, between 237 and 174.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Carnian to Toarcian (237 to 174.7 million years ago)
